Being called to the exercise of his office at an age when most young men are only beginning to qualify themselves for it, he did not have time to make very considerable progress in the learned languages.
But this deficiency was amply made up for by a lively and fertile genius, by fervent zeal, and by a forceful and most persuasive delivery.

And though in the pulpit he often found it necessary to “persuade men” by “the terrors of the Lord,” he had nothing gloomy in his nature, being singularly cheerful, as well as charitable and tenderhearted.
He was as ready to relieve the bodily needs as the spiritual needs of those who came to him.
It ought also to be observed that he constantly urged every moral duty upon his hearers, particularly diligence in their various callings and obedience to their superiors.

He endeavored, by the most extraordinary efforts of preaching in different places, and even in the open fields, to rouse the lower classes of people from the utmost degree of inattention and ignorance to a sense of religion.
For this, and for his other labors, the name of GEORGE WHITEFIELD will long be remembered with esteem and veneration.”
3. That both these accounts are just and impartial will readily be granted; that is, as far as they go.
But they go little further than the outside of his character.
They show you the preacher, but not the man, the Christian, the saint of God.
May I be permitted to add a little on this subject, from a personal acquaintance of nearly forty years?
Indeed, I am fully aware how difficult it is to speak on so delicate a subject; what prudence is required to avoid both extremes, to say neither too little nor too much!
No, I know it is impossible to speak at all, to say either less or more, without incurring from some the former censure, and from others the latter.
Some will seriously think that too little is said; and others, that it is too much.
But without paying attention to this, I will speak just what I know, before Him to whom we must all give an account.
4. Mention has already been made of his unparalleled zeal, his tireless activity, his tenderheartedness toward the afflicted, and his charitableness toward the poor.
But should we not also mention his deep gratitude to all whom God had used as instruments of good to him? — of whom he did not cease to speak in the most respectful manner, even to his dying day.
Should we not mention that he had a heart capable of the most generous and the most tender friendship?
I have frequently thought that this, above all others, was the distinguishing part of his character.
How few have we known of so kind a temper, of such large and flowing affections!
Was it not chiefly by this that the hearts of others were so remarkably drawn and knit to him?
Can anything but love give birth to love?
This shone in his very face, and continually breathed in all his words, whether in public or in private.
Was it not this which, quick and penetrating as lightning, flew from heart to heart? which gave that life to his sermons, his conversations, his letters?
You are witnesses!
5. But away with the vile misconstruction of men of corrupt minds, who know of no love but what is earthly and sensual!
Let it be remembered, at the same time, that he was endowed with the most delicate and unblemished modesty.
His office called him to converse very frequently and at length with women as well as men; and those of every age and condition.
But his whole behavior toward them was a practical commentary on that advice of St. Paul to Timothy: “Appeal to the elder women as mothers, the younger as sisters, with all purity.”

6. Meanwhile, how suited to the friendliness of his spirit was the frankness and openness of his conversation! — although it was as far removed from rudeness on the one hand as from guile [and disguise] on the other.
Was not this frankness at once a fruit and a proof of his courage and fearlessness?

Armed with these, he did not fear the faces of men, but “used great plainness of speech” to persons of every rank and condition, high and low, rich and poor; endeavoring only “by the manifestation of the truth to commend himself to every man’s conscience in the sight of God.”
7. Nor was he afraid of labor or pain, any more than of “what man [could] do to him”; being equally

blocks.x: Patient in bearing ill and in doing well.

s: And this appeared in the steadiness with which he pursued whatever he undertook for his Master’s sake.
Witness one instance for all — the Orphan House in Georgia, which he began and completed in spite of all discouragements.
Indeed, in whatever concerned himself he was pliant and flexible.
In such a case he was “easy to be entreated”; easy either to be convinced or to be persuaded.
But he was immovable in the things of God, or wherever his conscience was concerned.
None could persuade him, any more than frighten him, to depart in the least point from that integrity which was inseparable from his whole character, and which governed all his words and actions.
In this he did

blocks.x:
Stand like an iron pillar strong,
And steadfast as a wall of brass.

s: 8. If it is asked what was the foundation of this integrity, or of his sincerity, courage, patience, and every other valuable and lovely quality, it is easy to give the answer.

It was not the excellence of his natural temperament, not the strength of his understanding; it was not the force of education; no, nor the advice of his friends: it was nothing other than faith in a bleeding Lord; “faith of the operation of God.”
It was “a lively hope of an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and that never fades away.”
It was “the love of God spread abroad in his heart by the Holy Spirit who was given to him,” filling his soul with tender, disinterested love for every child of man.
From this source arose that torrent of eloquence which frequently swept away all before it; from this came that astonishing force of persuasion which the most hardened sinners could not resist.
This it was which often made his “head as waters, and his eyes a fountain of tears.”

This it was which enabled him to pour out his soul in prayer in a manner peculiar to himself, with such fullness and ease united together, with such strength and variety both of thought and of expression.

9. I may close this point by observing what an honor it pleased God to put upon His faithful servant, by allowing him to declare His everlasting gospel in so many different countries, to such numbers of people, and with so great an effect on so many of their precious souls!
Have we read or heard of any person since the Apostles who testified to the gospel of the grace of God through so widely extended a space, through so large a part of the habitable world?
Have we read or heard of any person who called so many thousands, so many myriads, of sinners to repentance?
Above all, have we read or heard of any who has been a blessed instrument in His hand of bringing so many sinners from “darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God”?
It is true that, were we to talk this way to the fashionable world, we would be judged to speak like barbarians.
But you understand the language of the country to which you are going, and where our dear friend has gone a little before us.
III. But how shall we make good use of this solemn providence?
This is the third thing we have to consider.
And the answer to this important question is easy (may God write it in all our hearts!).
By keeping close to the grand doctrines which he delivered; and by drinking in his spirit.
1. And, first, let us keep close to the grand scriptural doctrines which he delivered everywhere.
There are many doctrines of a less essential nature about which even the sincere children of God (such is the present weakness of human understanding) are divided, and have been for many ages.
In these matters we may think and let others think; we may “agree to disagree.”
But meanwhile, let us hold fast the essentials of “the faith which was once delivered to the saints,” and which this champion of God so strongly insisted on, at all times and in all places!
2. His fundamental point was, “Give God all the glory for whatever is good in man”; and, “In the business of salvation, set Christ as high and man as low as possible.”
With this point he and his friends at Oxford, the original Methodists, so called, set out.
Their grand principle was: there is no power (by nature) and no merit in man.
They insisted that all power to think, speak, or act rightly is in and from the Spirit of Christ; and all merit is (not in man, however high in grace, but merely) in the blood of Christ.
So he and they taught: there is no power in man, until it is given him from above, to do one good work, to speak one good word, or to form one good desire.
For it is not enough to say that all men are sick with sin: no, we are all “dead in trespasses and sins.”
It follows that all the children of men are “by nature children of wrath.”
We are all “guilty before God,” liable to death, temporal and eternal.
3. And we are all helpless, with regard both to the power and to the guilt of sin.
“For who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean one?”
None less than the Almighty.
Who can raise those who are dead, spiritually dead in sin?
None but He who raised us from the dust of the earth.
But on what grounds will He do this?
“Not on account of works of righteousness that we have done.”
“The dead cannot praise You, O Lord”; nor can they do anything for the sake of which they should be raised to life.
Whatever God does, therefore, He does merely for the sake of His well-beloved Son: “He was wounded for our transgressions, He was bruised for our iniquities.”
He Himself “bore” all “our sins in His own body on the tree.”
He “was delivered up for our offenses, and was raised again for our justification.”
Here, then, is the sole meritorious cause of every blessing we do or can enjoy; in particular of our pardon and acceptance with God, of our full and free justification.
But by what means do we come to have a share in what Christ has done and suffered?
“Not by works, so that no man may boast”; but by faith alone.
“We conclude,” says the Apostle, “that a man is justified by faith, without the works of the law.”
And “to as many as” thus “receive Him, He gives power to become the sons of God, even to those who believe in His name; who are born, not of the will of man, but of God.”
4. And “unless a man is” thus “born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”
But all who are thus “born of the Spirit” have “the kingdom of God within them.”
Christ sets up His kingdom in their hearts: “righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.”
That “mind is in them which was in Christ Jesus,” enabling them to “walk as Christ also walked.”
His indwelling Spirit makes them both holy in heart and “holy in all manner of conduct.”
But still, since all this is a free gift, through the righteousness and blood of Christ, there is eternally the same reason to remember: “He that glories, let him glory in the Lord.”
5. You are not unaware that these are the fundamental doctrines which he insisted on everywhere.
And may they not be summed up, as it were, in two words — the new birth, and justification by faith?
Let us insist on these with all boldness, at all times and in all places — in public (those of us who are called to it), and at every opportunity in private.
Keep close to these good, old, unfashionable doctrines, however many contradict and blaspheme.
Go on, my brethren, in the “name of the Lord, and in the power of His might.”
With all care and diligence “keep safe that which is committed to your trust,” knowing that “heaven and earth will pass away, but this truth will not pass away.”
6. But will it be enough to keep close to his doctrines, however pure they are?
Is there not a point of still greater importance than this, namely, to drink in his spirit? — in this to be a follower of him, even as he was of Christ?
Without this, the purity of our doctrines would only increase our condemnation.
This, therefore, is the principal thing — to copy his spirit.
And granting that in some points we must be content to admire what we cannot imitate, yet in many others we may, through the same free grace, be partakers of the same blessing.

Conscious, then, of your own needs and of His bountiful love, who “gives liberally and does not upbraid,” cry to Him who works all in all for a measure of the same precious faith; of the same zeal and activity; the same tenderheartedness, charitableness, and heartfelt mercy.
Wrestle with God for some measure of the same grateful, friendly, affectionate temper; of the same openness, simplicity, and godly sincerity; “love without pretense.”
Wrestle on, until the power from on high works in you the same steady courage and patience; and above all, because it is the crown of all, the same unvarying integrity!
7. Is there any other fruit of the grace of God with which he was eminently endowed, and the lack of which among the children of God he frequently and passionately lamented?

There is one, that is, catholic love: that sincere and tender affection which is due to all those who, we have reason to believe, are children of God by faith; in other words, all those, in every denomination, who “fear God and work righteousness.”
He longed to see all who had “tasted of the good word” be of a true catholic spirit — a word little understood, and still less experienced, by many who have it frequently in their mouths.
Who is the one who answers to this description?
Who is the man of a catholic spirit?

One who loves as friends, as brethren in the Lord, as joint partakers of the present kingdom of heaven, and fellow heirs of His eternal kingdom, all, of whatever opinion, mode of worship, or congregation, who believe in the Lord Jesus; who love God and man; who, rejoicing to please God and fearing to offend Him, are careful to abstain from evil, and zealous for good works.

He is a man of a truly catholic spirit who bears all these continually on his heart; who, having an inexpressible tenderness for their persons and an earnest desire for their welfare, does not cease to commend them to God in prayer, as well as to plead their cause before men; who speaks comfortingly to them, and labors by all his words to strengthen their hands in God.
He assists them to the utmost of his power in all things, spiritual and temporal; he is ready to “spend and be spent” for them; yes, “to lay down his life for his brethren.”
8. How lovely a character this is!
How desirable to every child of God!
But why, then, is it so rarely found?
How is it that there are so few instances of it?
Indeed, supposing we have tasted the love of God, how can any of us rest until it is our own?
Why, there is a subtle device by which Satan persuades thousands that they may stop short of it and yet be guiltless.
It is well if many who are present here are not in this “snare of the devil, taken captive at his will.”
“Oh yes,” says one, “I have all this love for those I believe to be children of God; but I will never believe that anyone is a child of God who belongs to that vile congregation!
Can he, do you think, be a child of God who holds such detestable opinions? or he who joins in such senseless and superstitious, if not idolatrous, worship?”
So we can justify ourselves in one sin by adding a second to it!
We excuse the lack of love in ourselves by laying the blame on others!
To disguise our own devilish temper, we pronounce our brethren children of the devil!
Oh, beware of this! — and if you are already caught in the snare, escape out of it as soon as possible!

Go and learn that truly catholic love which “is not rash,” or hasty in judging; that love which “thinks no evil”; which “believes and hopes all things”; which makes all the allowances for others that we desire others to make for us!
Then we shall recognize the grace of God which is in every man, whatever his opinion or mode of worship: then all who fear God will be near and dear to us “in the tender affection of Jesus Christ.”
9. Was not this the spirit of our dear friend?
And why should it not be ours?
O You God of love, how long shall Your people be a byword among the heathen?
How long shall they laugh us to scorn, and say, “See how these Christians love one another!”
When will You roll away our reproach?
Shall the sword devour forever?
How long will it be before You bid Your people return from “following each other”?
Now, at least, “let all the people stand still, and pursue their brethren no more!”
But whatever others do, let all of us, my brethren, hear the voice of him who, being dead, still speaks!
Suppose you hear him say: “Now, at least, be followers of me as I was of Christ!
Let brother “no more lift up sword against brother, nor know war any more!”
Rather, put on, as the elect of God, heartfelt mercy, humility of mind, brotherly kindness, gentleness, long-suffering, bearing with one another in love.
Let the time past suffice for strife, envy, and contention; for biting and devouring one another.
Blessed be God that you have not long ago been consumed by one another!
From now on keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”
10. O God, with You no word is impossible!
You do whatever pleases You!
Oh, that You would cause the mantle of Your prophet, whom You have taken up, now to fall upon us who remain!
“Where is the Lord, the God of Elijah?”
Let his spirit rest upon these Your servants!
Show that You are the God who answers by fire!
Let the fire of Your love fall on every heart!
And because we love You, let us love one another with a “love stronger than death!”
Take away from us “all anger, and wrath, and bitterness; all clamor and evil speaking!”
Let Your Spirit so rest upon us that from this hour we may be “kind to each other, tender-hearted, forgiving one another, even as God, for Christ’s sake, has forgiven us!”

1 Servant of God, well done!
Your glorious warfare’s past;
The battle’s fought, the race is won,
And you are crowned at last;
Of all your heart’s desire
Triumphantly possessed,
Lodged by the ministering choir
In your Redeemer’s breast.

2 In condescending love,
Your ceaseless prayer He heard;
And called you suddenly away
To your complete reward:
Ready to bring the peace,
Your beautiful feet were shod,
When mercy signed your soul’s release,
And caught you up to God.

3 With saints enthroned on high,
You now your Lord proclaim,
And still “To God salvation!” cry,
“Salvation to the Lamb!”
O happy, happy soul!
In ecstasies of praise,

4 Redeemed from earth and pain,
Ah! when shall we ascend,
And all in Jesus’ presence reign
With our translated friend?

And, when in You complete,
